weeklyHoursLimit.label: Work limit in the busiest month
weeklyHoursLimit.hint: For the whole farm together. Checked in the pessimistic scenario (settings at the bottom of the list).

minimumNetIncome.label: Minimum net income in the pessimistic scenario

fullTimeHoursPerYear.label: Hours of a full-time job per year
fullTimeHoursPerYear.hint: About 40 h a week with holidays. On a farm it usually ends up being more.

leasedHa.label: Leased land (extra)
leasedHa.hint: Added to meadow and fields. Rent below.

leaseRentPerHa.label: Land rent
leaseRentPerHa.hint: State land (KOWR) in 2024: on average about 12 dt of wheat per ha (about 1,100 PLN). Private meadows can be cheaper.

soilClassIIIShare.label: Class III soils
soilClassIIIShare.hint: Yields in the “Yields” group are for class IV soil. Class III gives more: cereals about +20%, meadows about +10%.

soilClassVShare.label: Class V soils
soilClassVShare.hint: Class V: cereals and clover about −25%, meadows and pastures about −15% (grasses cope with poorer soil better than cereals). The rest is class IV. An estimate.

soilClassVIShare.label: Class VI soils
soilClassVIShare.hint: Class VI: cereals about −45%, grasses about −30%. Better used for pasture, trees or sheep than for cereals.

rotationFields.label: Crop rotation: number of fields (years)
rotationFields.hint: Cereals and clover move one field further every year. Details in the “Crop rotation” section.

cerealShare.label: Cereals and legumes in the rotation
cerealShare.hint: The rest of the arable land is clover with grass for hay. In organic farming it is the source of nitrogen, so 100% cereals does not work in the long run.

rootCrops.label: Root crops in the rotation (potatoes, fodder beet)
rootCrops.hint: One field of the rotation before the last oats, as in the Norfolk four-course rotation: clover → cereal → root crops → oats with undersown clover. Root crops get the manure, hoeing cleans the field of weeds, and the crop replaces part of the grain fed to cows and pigs. Needs at least two cereal years in the rotation.

milkPerCow.label: Milk per cow
milkPerCow.hint: Jersey without grain: 3,500–4,000 l. 100% grass-fed farms in the US: about 3,800 kg on average.

onceADayMilking.label: Once-a-day milking (New Zealand style)
onceADayMilking.hint: About 20% less milk, but milking and parlour cleaning once a day: about 35% less work per cow and 40% less fixed work. The cows are in better condition. In New Zealand studies milk falls by 10–30%, and Jerseys lose less than Holsteins.

cheeseShare.label: Share of that milk made into cheese

milkPrice.label: Price of raw milk sold by the farmer
milkPrice.hint: Dairies paid about 1.5–2.6 PLN/l in 2026. Raw milk sold by the farmer usually 3–6 PLN/l; A2A2 Jersey milk can fetch more in town. Selling raw milk is a direct sale (registered with the district vet), not farm retail.

cheesePrice.label: Price of hard cheese
cheesePrice.hint: An assumption. Aged farmhouse cheeses usually sell for about 60–150 PLN/kg depending on the cheese, its age and the sales channel; current prices could not be confirmed. Enter your own price.

cheeseYield.label: Cheese yield
cheeseYield.hint: Cheddar from Jersey milk: about 12.5 kg, from Holstein about 10.1 kg. A little less after ageing.

lactationsPerCow.label: Average number of lactations per cow

ownBull.label: Own bull (otherwise AI or a borrowed bull)

cullCowPrice.label: Cull cow for slaughter
cullCowPrice.hint: Slaughter cattle at buyers: 12.55 PLN/kg live weight (July 2026, ZSRIR); cows less. A Jersey weighs about 400 kg.

eggsPerHen.label: Laying rate
eggsPerHen.hint: Green-legged Partridge: about 180–200 eggs a year (a conservation breed); other native breeds 190–230; commercial hybrids on range 250–280.

eggPrice.label: Price of an egg
eggPrice.hint: Median of 49 adverts for farm eggs on OLX (Nov 2026): 1.20 PLN each; ŚODR (May 2026): 1.22 PLN on average (0.60–2.00). Free-range Green-legged eggs usually sell higher to regular customers: 1.4–2 PLN.

henFeedGramsPerDay.label: Feed per hen
henFeedGramsPerDay.hint: A Green-legged hen (about 1.6–2 kg) eats about 100–120 g a day, commercial hens 120–130 g; a good range lowers the amount.

rangeFeedSaving.label: Feed saved by foraging on the range

ownHatching.label: Own hatching (cockerels in the flock, incubator)
ownHatching.hint: Replacement pullets from your own eggs; cockerels reared and sold as soup birds. Vaccinate the chicks against Marek’s disease (agree it with your vet).

cockerelPrice.label: Soup cockerel
cockerelPrice.hint: An assumption; check locally. Green-legged Partridge: about 16–20 weeks to a carcass of about 1.5 kg.

hatchingHoursPerChick.label: Hatching and rearing: work per chick
hatchingHoursPerChick.hint: Counts about 2 chicks for every pullet added to the flock (half are cockerels).

winterPolytunnel.label: Poultry in a polytunnel in winter (deep litter)
winterPolytunnel.hint: The vegetable tunnel from November to March: a place for the poultry during a housing order, compost for spring. Openings covered with netting, a heated drinker, netting dug in along the edges.

tunnelBeddingCostPerHen.label: Sawdust or wood chips for the tunnel

pulletPrice.label: Price of a pullet (point of lay)

broilerPricePerKg.label: Carcass price
broilerPricePerKg.hint: Broiler carcasses wholesale: 9.06 PLN/kg (July 2026, ZSRIR). Free-range chicken straight from the farmer: usually about 25–40 PLN/kg.

broilerFeedKg.label: Feed per broiler
broilerFeedKg.hint: Slow-growing breeds on range to a carcass of about 2.3 kg: about 7–9 kg of feed per bird; a grassy range gives the lower end.

goosePrice.label: Price of a goose
goosePrice.hint: Fattened geese at buyers: 16.09 PLN/kg live weight (July 2026, ZSRIR). An oat-fed farm goose has a carcass of about 4–4.5 kg.

ducks.label: Ducks
ducks.hint: They need bathing water (a paddling pool) and foul the drinkers badly. Good at eating slugs.

duckPricePerKg.label: Duck: carcass price
duckPricePerKg.hint: Organic in online shops about 68 PLN/kg (3.2 kg carcass, Wolny Wypas 2026). Usually cheaper from the farmer.

turkeys.label: Turkeys
turkeys.hint: Keep them apart from hens and on different ground: blackhead (histomoniasis), carried by hens, can kill up to 100% of a turkey flock. There is practically no treatment.

turkeyPricePerKg.label: Turkey: carcass price
turkeyPricePerKg.hint: Organic in shops about 82 PLN/kg (carcass about 8 kg). Demand rises for Christmas and Thanksgiving.

guineaFowl.label: Guinea fowl
guineaFowl.hint: Noisy, but they scare off hawks and eat insects. They grow slowly: at least about 5 months.

guineaFowlPricePerKg.label: Guinea fowl: carcass price
guineaFowlPricePerKg.hint: Organic about 65 PLN/kg (Wolny Wypas, a farm described by topagrar in 2024).

rabbitPrice.label: Price of a rabbit carcass
rabbitPrice.hint: Carcass about 1.5–2 kg. Rabbits in the Świętokrzyskie region (May 2026): about 30 PLN/kg on average, from 6.5 to 55 PLN (ŚODR).

sucklerCows.label: Suckler cows (Angus)
sucklerCows.hint: For comparison: in this model the least profitable per hectare, but little work and good on poorer meadows. Needs a quiet bull or AI.

weanersSoldShare.label: Calves sold as weaners
weanersSoldShare.hint: Weaners at about 7–8 months, in autumn. The rest stay as finishers until about 2 years.

weanerPricePerKg.label: Weaner: price
weanerPricePerKg.hint: Average price of slaughter cattle in April 2026: 14.13 PLN/kg live weight (KOWR). Beef-breed weaners usually fetch more per kg. An assumption.

finishersSoldAsMeatShare.label: Finishers sold as boxed meat
finishersSoldAsMeatShare.hint: Slaughter at an abattoir, sale under farm retail rules. The rest sold live.

beefBoxPricePerKg.label: Boxed beef
beefBoxPricePerKg.hint: Average per kg of carcass (mixed cuts). Young-bull quarters at buyers: 27.54 PLN/kg (KOWR, April 2026).

beefCattleCostPerHead.label: Vet, ear tags, minerals, hoof care

finisherSlaughterCost.label: Slaughter, butchery, transport of a finisher

lambingsPerEwe.label: Lambings per ewe per year
lambingsPerEwe.hint: Dorpers can lamb 3 times in 2 years (1.5 a year). Two lambings a year are impossible: pregnancy lasts about 146–150 days. With more frequent lambing, litter size is often about 25% lower, and more hay and work are needed in winter.

lambLivePrice.label: Price of a lamb sold live
lambLivePrice.hint: An assumption (about 40 kg live weight at about 13–14 PLN/kg). World sheep-meat prices were at record highs in 2026.

lambsSoldAsMeatShare.label: Lambs sold as meat (farm retail)
lambsSoldAsMeatShare.hint: The rest are sold live. Meat: slaughter at an abattoir, a whole carcass or boxes for customers.

lambLiveWeightKg.label: Lamb weight at sale or slaughter

lambMeatPricePerKg.label: Price of lamb for customers
lambMeatPricePerKg.hint: Farmers’ adverts: usually 30–60 PLN/kg (median about 40 PLN). Farm shops: 43–52 PLN/kg for a whole carcass.

lambKillingOut.label: Killing-out percentage (carcass of live weight)
lambKillingOut.hint: Meat crossbreds about 46%, Dorper about 50%, native sheep kept extensively as little as about 36%.

lambSlaughterCost.label: Contract slaughter at an abattoir
lambSlaughterCost.hint: An assumption. Ask the abattoir for its price list.

lambsPerAbattoirTrip.label: Lambs in one batch for slaughter
lambsPerAbattoirTrip.hint: Each batch means 2 trips: delivering the live lambs and collecting the chilled carcasses.

trailerCostPerKm.label: Cost of driving with a trailer

kidsSoldShare.label: Kids sold for meat
kidsSoldShare.hint: The other kids become dog food. Goats must be slaughtered at an abattoir and sold under farm retail rules. Kid meat sells mainly at Easter and to customers from the Balkans and the Middle East.

kidMeatPricePerKg.label: Kid meat
kidMeatPricePerKg.hint: An assumption for direct sales; check locally.

pigsForSale.label: Pigs for sale
pigsForSale.hint: Half carcasses or boxes under farm retail rules; slaughter only at an abattoir. African swine fever is present in Lower Silesia: ask the district vet whether pigs may be kept outdoors in your district and what the biosecurity rules are (e.g. a double fence).

porkBoxPricePerKg.label: Boxed pork
porkBoxPricePerKg.hint: Half carcasses wholesale only 6.96 PLN/kg, live pigs 4.83 PLN/kg (July 2026, ZSRIR). Outdoor pork in boxes for regular customers: about 15–35 PLN/kg. An assumption.

horses.label: Horses (just in case)
horses.hint: A horse eats about 3 t of dry matter in hay and grass a year and about 200 kg of oats in light work.

horseCost.label: Horse: farrier, vet, minerals
horseCost.hint: Hoof trimming from about 50 PLN, vaccination 70–90 PLN, worming 40–50 PLN, check-up 200–300 PLN (kb.pl, 2026).

marketGardenHa.label: Vegetables for sale (CSA, market)
marketGardenHa.hint: Land taken from the arable fields. The Dobrzyń Vegetables CSA: about 5 ha and over 530 members paying 1,480–1,740 PLN a season.

vegetableSalesPerHa.label: Vegetable sales per hectare
vegetableSalesPerHa.hint: An assumption. The Dobrzyń CSA takes about 170,000 PLN per ha in shares. The best small market gardens in the US and Canada sell 100,000 USD per acre; typical CSAs there under 40,000 USD.

vegetableHoursPerHa.label: Work on vegetables
vegetableHoursPerHa.hint: Hand growing with a tunnel and selling: small market gardens usually need 4,000–6,000 h per hectare (1–1.5 people per half hectare). Less with simpler growing and bigger beds.

fruitSoldShare.label: Orchard fruit for sale
fruitSoldShare.hint: Fresh or as juice from a contract press. The rest for the household. The orchard is set under “Land”.

orchardYield.label: Orchard yield
orchardYield.hint: An assumption for an extensive orchard in full bearing. A new orchard starts bearing after about 4–6 years and then crops more heavily every other year.

fruitPricePerKg.label: Revenue per kg of fruit
fruitPricePerKg.hint: An average for fresh fruit and juice. 1 kg of apples gives about 0.6–0.7 l of juice. An assumption.

mushroomLogs.label: Logs for oyster mushrooms
mushroomLogs.hint: Sections 30–40 cm long and 20–50 cm across, almost any hardwood. They lie in the shade under trees and take no field space. The harvest is about 20% of the wood’s weight over 2–5 years (Dr M. Siwulski, Poznań University of Life Sciences).

mushroomYieldPerLog.label: Mushrooms per log
mushroomYieldPerLog.hint: A log of about 20 kg × 20% over about 3 years gives about 1.3 kg a year. Shiitake on oak or beech yields less but sells higher.

mushroomPrice.label: Mushroom price
mushroomPrice.hint: An assumption for log-grown oyster mushrooms sold direct.

beehives.label: Beehives (colonies)
beehives.hint: They take no land and pollinate the orchard and clover.

honeyPerHive.label: Honey per hive
honeyPerHive.hint: In Poland about 15–20 kg per hive on average; much less in poor years.

honeyPrice.label: Honey price in direct sales
honeyPrice.hint: Average retail prices in 2025: multifloral about 35.5 PLN/kg, honeydew about 64 PLN, heather about 91 PLN (INHORT).

hiveCost.label: Cash cost of a hive (feed, treatments, jars)

geeseProcessedShare.label: Geese processed (smoked breast, smoked cuts, lard)

processedValuePerGoose.label: Products from one goose
processedValuePerGoose.hint: E.g. about 0.8 kg of smoked goose breast at 180–200 PLN plus smoked legs, lard and pâté. Organic smoked breast from pastured geese: 200 PLN/kg (Manufaktura Dobra, 2026).

lambProcessedShare.label: Lamb processed (sausages, kabanos, ham)
lambProcessedShare.hint: From the lambs that go to the abattoir. Meat of hoofed animals must come from an abattoir.

processedValuePerLambKg.label: Products per kg of lamb carcass
processedValuePerLambKg.hint: Value of the products per kg of carcass with bones, after losses in butchery and smoking. An assumption.

processingMaterialsShare.label: Materials: spices, casings, jars, vacuum bags, labels

shippedShare.label: Products shipped by courier
shippedShare.hint: Polish farm retail (RHD) rules allow distance selling to consumers if the right temperature is kept in transport. The rest is collected in person or sold at the market.

parcelCost.label: Parcel: insulated box, ice packs, courier
parcelCost.hint: An assumption. Ask couriers about chilled food parcels.

grazingDays.label: Grazing days per year
grazingDays.hint: Around Lwówek usually from about 20 April to the end of October.

mixedGrazingBonus.label: Sheep after cows: better use of the pasture
mixedGrazingBonus.hint: Grazing cattle and sheep together or one after the other: about 10% more pasture capacity (Nolan and Connolly 1989). Full effect from about 1.5 sheep per head of cattle.

pastureYield.label: Pasture yield (eaten)
pastureYield.hint: Polish pastures average about 3.4 t of hay/ha (about 2.9 t DM; ITP), but that average includes neglected ones. Rotational grazing with clover in the sward: about 4–6 t DM eaten; potential 2.5–8 t of hay/ha.

meadowYield.label: Meadow yield (2 cuts)
meadowYield.hint: Polish meadows average about 4.6 t of hay/ha (about 3.9 t DM; ITP, 2005–2009); extensive ones with 1 cut about 2.5 t of hay. A good meadow manured with farmyard manure: 4–6 t DM.

cloverYield.label: Clover-grass yield
cloverYield.hint: Red clover with grasses, 2–3 cuts: usually 6–9 t DM/ha, on organic farms and poorer soils about 5–7.

cerealYield.label: Cereal and mixture yield (organic)
cerealYield.hint: Organic farms: cereals about 1.5–3 t/ha (IUNG). On class IV soil after clover and manure about 2.5–3.5; cereal-legume mixtures in IUNG trials 2.6–4.9 t/ha. Yield for class IV; soil classes are set under “Land”.

strawYield.label: Straw yield
strawYield.hint: Usually about 1–1.2 t of straw per 1 t of grain; rye and triticale more, oats with peas less.

rootCropYield.label: Root crop yield as grain equivalent
rootCropYield.hint: Organic fodder beet: 40–60 t/ha fresh weight, i.e. about 6–9 t of dry matter; organic potatoes 15–25 t/ha. Counted as feed-grain equivalent, because the energy in beet dry matter is close to barley.

grazingMoveIntervalDays.label: Move the cows to a new paddock every
grazingMoveIntervalDays.hint: 0.5 means twice a day, after morning and evening milking. Moving more often leaves less ungrazed grass and spreads dung more evenly: about +4% grass eaten with moves twice a day, −7% every 3 days, −16% once a week. It takes more work with polywire and water, though. Salatin and Perkins move their cattle daily.

pastureRestDays.label: Back to the same paddock after
pastureRestDays.hint: The paddock’s rest. In spring 20–30 days is enough, in summer and drought 40–60 (Salatin: up to 60 days, until the grass rebuilds its roots). Less than 25 days weakens the sward; with longer rests the grass gets old. The number of paddocks is the rest divided by the days in one paddock, plus one.

bullCost.label: Bull: purchase spread over years, vet

costPerEwe.label: Ewe: vet, ear tags, ram, hoof care

fixedCosts.label: Farmers’ social insurance (KRUS), land tax, insurance, organic certificate
fixedCosts.hint: KRUS in 2026: about 256 PLN a month per person (178 PLN pension and disability, 78 PLN accident and sickness), about 6,200 PLN a year for 2 people. Agricultural land tax 2026: 166 PLN per conversion hectare. Plus the organic certificate, liability insurance and building insurance.

salesCosts.label: Selling: fuel for deliveries, market fees

energyCosts.label: Electricity and water (cooling, washing, general)
energyCosts.hint: Milk cooling, hot water for washing the milking machine, the cheese room, the pump and henhouse lighting: about 3,000–4,000 kWh a year at about 1 PLN/kWh. Without cows and a cheese room usually about 2,000 PLN.

sellSurplusGrain.label: Sell surplus grain after harvest
sellSurplusGrain.hint: Grain beyond what the animals need and the reserve for a poorer year goes to a buyer or a neighbour. Without animals all the grain is sold.

grainSalePrice.label: Selling price of organic grain
grainSalePrice.hint: Conventional triticale at buyers: about 760–785 PLN/t (KOWR, Sept–Oct 2026), rye about 660–680 PLN/t. Organic grain usually sells 30–50% higher, but small lots have to be delivered or sold to neighbouring organic farms.

feedReserveShare.label: Grain and straw reserve above needs
feedReserveShare.hint: This much above the animals’ yearly needs stays in store for a poorer year. Grain above the reserve is sold and surplus straw is ploughed in.

sawdustForStraw.label: Replace missing straw with sawdust or wood chips
sawdustForStraw.hint: Instead of buying straw, you top up the bedding with sawdust from a sawmill. On an organic farm only from untreated wood. Manure with sawdust rots more slowly: compost it longer before spreading.

sawdustPrice.label: Sawdust or wood chips
sawdustPrice.hint: About 40–80 PLN/m³ from a sawmill; 1 m³ of sawdust weighs about 0.2–0.25 t. Sometimes free if you collect it.

sawdustPerStrawTonne.label: Sawdust instead of 1 t of straw
sawdustPerStrawTonne.hint: Sawdust absorbs about as much as straw per kilogram. An assumption.

rootCropCostPerHa.label: Root crops: cost above ordinary arable
rootCropCostPerHa.hint: Seed potatoes or beet seed, contract planting and lifting, storage. Usually 1,500–4,000 PLN/ha more than a cereal.

investHenHouse.label: Mobile henhouse (by the farmyard in winter)

investOtherPoultryShelters.label: Movable shelters: ducks, turkeys, guinea fowl
investOtherPoultryShelters.hint: A turkey counts as 3 places. Ducks usually in 2 batches a season.

investElectricFencing.label: Electric fencing
investElectricFencing.hint: With sheep and goats 30% more is counted (more wires, netting).

investDairy.label: Milking machine, cooling tank, milk room
investDairy.hint: Less if you convert the old cowshed.

investMachinery.label: Used implements for a small (C-360) tractor
investMachinery.hint: Mower, tedder, rake, seed drill, harrow. Less if you already have some.

investBeehive.label: Hive with equipment and a colony

investPoultryTunnel.label: Tunnel: netting, heated drinkers, lamps
investPoultryTunnel.hint: With an existing tunnel. A new 6 × 20 m tunnel costs much more.

investHorseStable.label: Shelter or stable for a horse

investProcessingRoom.label: Smokehouse, cold store, vacuum packer, room
investProcessingRoom.hint: An assumption. The room must meet hygiene requirements and be registered with the district vet.

investOther.label: Other investments (not counted elsewhere)
investOther.hint: Anything not on the list above: a well, a track, a utility connection, a farm building, a van. The amount can also be typed in the investments table.

investOtherLifetimeYears.label: Other investments: years of use
investOtherLifetimeYears.hint: Depreciation is the amount divided by this many years.

organicPayment.label: Organic payment (once in the organic system)

livestockDensityBonus.label: Bonus for mixed crop and livestock farming (0.5–1.5 LU/ha)

catchCrops.label: Winter catch crops and undersowing (“Carbon farming” eco-scheme, 5 points/ha)
catchCrops.hint: A mixture of at least 2 species sown by 1 October and kept until 15 February; legumes undersown in oats kept at least 8 weeks after harvest. No plant protection products. The “Crop rotation” section shows where they fit in the rotation.

carbonManure.label: Manure worked into the soil within 12 h (2 points/ha)
carbonManure.hint: Geotagged photos in the ARiMR mobile app or a statement with dates within 14 days.

carbonCropDiversity.label: Diverse crop structure (3 points per ha of arable land)
carbonCropDiversity.hint: At least 3 crops, cereals at most 65%, crops that build organic matter (e.g. clover) at least 20%. Checked against your rotation.

ecoSchemePointValue.label: Value of an eco-scheme point
ecoSchemePointValue.hint: In 2026 an estimated 92.76 PLN per point (ARiMR advance rates, September 2026); the final rate can differ slightly. Threshold: points at least 25% of farmland × 5 points.

catchCropCostPerHa.label: Catch crop: organic seed and sowing

catchCropForageYield.label: Catch crop: grazing in autumn and early spring
catchCropForageYield.hint: Sheep or heifers on the catch crop (rye with vetch) in autumn and March. Be careful with grazing before 15 February.

catchCropMix.label: Catch crop mixture (chosen in the crop rotation)

stubbleCrop.label: Stubble crop as green manure before a winter cereal (no payment)
stubbleCrop.hint: After an early harvest, when a winter cereal follows: mustard, phacelia or buckwheat for 6–7 weeks, then ploughed in in September. It does not meet the eco-scheme rules (the cover does not last until 15 February), but it improves the soil and feeds the geese.

stubbleCropMix.label: Stubble crop mixture (chosen in the crop rotation)

stubbleCropForageYield.label: Stubble crop: forage from grazing or a cut

extensiveGrasslandScheme.label: Eco-scheme: extensive grassland with livestock
extensiveGrasslandScheme.hint: Ask your advisory centre (ODR) whether it can be combined with the organic payment.

lessFavouredAreaRate.label: Less-favoured area payment (if the plots are in a zone)
lessFavouredAreaRate.hint: Lwówek Śląski municipality: only some precincts. 2026 rates: specific zone I 179 PLN, zone II 264 PLN, upland zone II with at least 0.3 LU/ha 676 PLN (e.g. Nagórze).

welfareCowsGrazing.label: Animal welfare: cows – grazing and bedding (about 380 PLN/head)

welfareCowsSpace.label: Animal welfare: cows – 20% more space in the shelter (about 640 PLN/head)
welfareCowsSpace.hint: Needs a big enough shelter; work out the floor area before building.

welfareSheepGoats.label: Animal welfare: sheep and goats (about 143 and 138 PLN/head)

hoursPerCow.label: Cows: per cow
hoursPerCow.hint: Per cow: grazing, moving, bedding, calves, treatment (plus the fixed parlour time). With 5 cows it comes to about 170 h per cow a year in total. Milking alone in large barns is about 20 h per cow (ITP), with a bucket milking machine in a small herd much more.

cheeseHoursPer100Litres.label: Cheesemaking
cheeseHoursPer100Litres.hint: Hard cheese: about 3–4 h per 100 l batch including cleaning; then care in the ageing room. Enter your own time after a few batches.

hoursPerHen.label: Hens: per hen
hoursPerHen.hint: Feeding, water, collecting eggs, moving the henhouse. With about 100–300 hens usually 1–2 h per hen a year including the fixed time and egg sales.

hoursPerBroiler.label: Broiler: rearing, slaughter, evisceration
hoursPerBroiler.hint: Missouri Extension (pastured): about 0.3 h per broiler with batches of 100, including slaughter; with 700 about 0.1 h. Here 0.6 h, including selling and learning at the start.

hoursPerEwe.label: Ewe
hoursPerEwe.hint: Meat sheep kept extensively: usually 5–10 h per ewe a year (lambing, feet, worming, shearing).

abattoirTripHours.label: Trip to the abattoir (there and back)

lambSalesHoursPerLamb.label: Selling lamb: phone calls, handing out boxes

rootCropHoursPerHa.label: Root crops: work
rootCropHoursPerHa.hint: Planting, hoeing and ridging, lifting, clamping. With contract planting and lifting about 60–120 h/ha, by hand much more.

paddockMoveHours.label: Moving to a new paddock: work
paddockMoveHours.hint: Moving the polywire and the trough, checking the fence. With a laneway with water and quick couplings it takes about 10–20 minutes. The work norms per cow assume one move a day, so only the difference counts here.

targetFromHouseholdBudget.label: Work out the minimum net income from the household budget
targetFromHouseholdBudget.hint: When on, the pessimistic threshold is calculated from the spending, margin and savings below, minus the 800+ child benefit. When off, the minimum slider in the “People” group applies.

householdMonthlySpending.label: Household spending
householdMonthlySpending.hint: An estimate for 5 people living frugally, with more than half of the food home-grown and their own firewood and water. Without KRUS and land tax, which are in the farm’s costs.

householdSavings.label: Savings: pension, emergency fund
householdSavings.hint: The KRUS pension will be low, so it is worth saving, e.g. in an IKZE retirement account.

openingCash.label: Cash in the account on 1 January
openingCash.hint: The balance in the cash-flow table starts from this amount.

childBenefitChildren.label: Children with 800+ benefit
childBenefitChildren.hint: 800 PLN a month per child under 18.

pessimisticPriceDrop.label: Selling prices lower by
pessimisticPriceDrop.hint: Applies to all prices: milk, cheese, eggs, meat, vegetables, fruit, mushrooms, honey and cured products.

pessimisticYieldDrop.label: Yields lower by
pessimisticYieldDrop.hint: Cereals, straw, meadow, pasture, clover, orchard, honey, mushrooms. A drought or a wet year.

pessimisticAnimalOutputDrop.label: Animal output lower by
pessimisticAnimalOutputDrop.hint: Milk per cow, laying rate, lambs and rabbits reared.

pessimisticExtraHours.label: Work takes longer by
pessimisticExtraHours.hint: All work norms. Illness, breakdowns, learning.

pessimisticCostIncrease.label: Running costs higher by
pessimisticCostIncrease.hint: Also the prices of bought grain, hay and straw. Rent is not changed.

loyalCustomerSpendPerMonth.label: Regular customer family: spending per month
loyalCustomerSpendPerMonth.hint: A family that buys a large part of its food from the farm: eggs every week, milk, cheese, a chicken, a meat box, a goose for Christmas. A family of 4 spends about 2,000–3,000 PLN a month on food, so 400–700 PLN is about a fifth.

occasionalCustomerSpendPerMonth.label: Single-product customer: spending per month
occasionalCustomerSpendPerMonth.hint: Someone who only buys eggs or a goose once a year. A few dozen PLN a month on average.

baleGrazing.label: Bale grazing in winter
baleGrazing.hint: Cattle and sheep winter in the field: hay bales set out in autumn, the polywire moved to the next ones every day. The dung stays where it falls and little bedding is needed, but about 10% of the hay is trampled. Milking cows come back for milking.

manureHoursPerTonne.label: Manure: loading and spreading
manureHoursPerTonne.hint: A loader on a C-360 and a small spreader: about 2–3 t per load, about 0.15–0.3 h per tonne.

riskYieldVolatility.label: Random years: yield variability
riskYieldVolatility.hint: Typical deviation of yields from the average from year to year (drought, a wet summer). On lighter soils and in organic farming usually 12–20%.

riskPriceVolatility.label: Random years: price and sales variability
riskPriceVolatility.hint: Direct-sale prices are steadier than prices at buyers, but every year some produce may not sell or may need discounting. Usually 5–15%.

riskAnimalVolatility.label: Random years: animal output variability
riskAnimalVolatility.hint: Milk, laying rate, lambs and rabbits reared in ordinary years.

riskBadYearChance.label: Random years: chance of a bad year for the animals
riskBadYearChance.hint: Disease in the herd, a poultry housing order during bird flu, or lost customers. In such a year animal output is about 25% lower. 5% means once in 20 years on average.

maximumProfit.label: Maximum profit
maximumProfit.note: All the family’s time, no weekly limit

presets.showPessimistic: Show everything in the pessimistic scenario

lubuskieAngus.label: Lubusz style: Angus on grass
lubuskieAngus.description: Beef farming as typical in the Lubusz region: Angus suckler cows on pasture all season, moved once a week, weaners sold in autumn, hay from the meadows in winter. Plus the extensive grassland eco-scheme and cattle payments. About 8 suckler cows fit on 14 ha, so it is a side income. In the region such herds usually farm 50–200 ha, often leased.

perkinsRidgedale.label: Ridgedale (R. Perkins)
perkinsRidgedale.description: Modelled on Richard Perkins’ Ridgedale farm in Sweden: an intensive no-dig market garden, broilers in movable pens, hens in a mobile henhouse, turkeys, sheep and a few beef cows in rotational grazing moved daily. Plus an orchard, oyster mushrooms among the trees and catch crops. A lot of work and direct selling, but many sources of income.

salatinPolyface.label: Polyface (J. Salatin)
salatinPolyface.description: Modelled on Joel Salatin’s Polyface: cattle moved daily, a paddock grazed again after about 60 days, a mobile henhouse following 3–4 days behind the cattle. Broilers in pens moved daily, turkeys, rabbits and a few pigs. Grass-finished beef sold in boxes. Salatin buys his grain; here it comes from the farm’s own fields.

grassDairy.label: Grass milk (Voisin, NZ)
grassDairy.description: Pasture dairying following André Voisin’s rational grazing and New Zealand practice: Jersey cows almost entirely on grass, a fresh paddock every day, about 35 days’ rest, once-a-day milking, most of the milk made into cheese. The pasture has as many hectares as the cows will eat; winter hay comes from clover-grass leys on the arable land, without a separate meadow. A mobile henhouse behind the cows uses grain from the farm’s own fields. Less milk, but much less time in the parlour.

sweetSpot.label: Sweet spot
sweetSpot.note: All 14 ha, most PLN per hour
sweetSpot.description: The result of searching thousands of combinations on 14 ha without leased land: the highest income per hour of work with at least 6,500 PLN a month in the pessimistic scenario, all the land in use (every feed with about a 5–10% reserve, no shortages) and a peak below 60 h a week. It came out as laying hens, ducks, a few geese and a few suckler cows with finishers sold in boxes, plus grazing moved every 3 days with long paddock rests. No dairy cows, because milking takes the most hours.

notes.grazingOrder:
Order on the pasture

The cows go in first and eat the top of the sward. 1–3 days later the sheep clean up the lower grasses and herbs. 3–4 days after the cows the mobile henhouse arrives: the hens scratch apart the cowpats, eat the fly larvae and fertilise. Cows and sheep mostly have different parasites, so this order breaks their life cycle.
notes.buildings:
Buildings: cheap and light

  • Old cowshed: milking parlour, dairy room, cheese room (they need a separate, washable room).
  • A frame shelter clad with OSB or boards, open to the east, on deep litter: cows and heifers.
  • A second shelter or an extension: sheep and goats, a night pen against wolves.
  • Mobile henhouses on skids, pulled by a C-360 tractor; in winter they stand by the farmyard.
notes.waterAndFencing:
Water and fencing

  • A PE pipe along the laneway with quick couplings every 2–3 paddocks, a portable trough.
  • Perimeter: 2–3 permanent wires (4–5 for sheep), polywire on portable posts inside.
  • An energiser with enough spare power, earthed at several points.

rotation.title: Crop rotation on arable land
rotation.intro: On an organic farm nitrogen comes from clover and manure, so part of the arable land is always under clover with grasses. You choose the number of fields below (or in the “Land” group), the cereal share with the slider. Click a year to see it on the plan.

catchCrops.title: Catch crops and eco-schemes
catchCrops.intro: A catch crop is green cover between two main crops: it protects the soil in winter, holds nitrogen, feeds soil life and gives the sheep forage. In the “Carbon farming” eco-scheme a winter catch crop or undersowing earns 5 points/ha, about 500 PLN/ha. You switch them on with the buttons by the rotation or in the “Payments” group.
catchCrops.requirements: Practice requirements (ARiMR, PODR 2025): at least 2 species, not cereals only; a winter catch crop sown by 1 Oct and kept until 15 Feb (mulching allowed after 15 Nov); an undersown legume kept until the next crop is sown or at least 8 weeks after harvest; no plant protection products. On an organic farm, organic seed (or permission for non-organic). Seed rates are approximate: check with the seed supplier. Whether the eco-scheme can be combined with the organic payment on the same plot, confirm with the agricultural advisory centre (ODR) before applying.
catchCrops.grainLegumeMixtures: In IUNG trials cereal-pulse mixtures gave about 2.6–4.9 t/ha and 16–19% protein (peas with wheat). Pulses make up 40–50% of the seed. It is worth supplementing the hens’ grain with whey from the cheese room (protein) and green forage from the range.

calendar.title: The farming year
calendar.intro: Calving and lambing in early spring, breeding in summer, hay in June, selling geese and cheese in autumn and before Christmas. Dates for the Lwówek area (grazing from about 20 April).

stages.title: How to start: three years
stages.intro: Each new enterprise only once the previous one is selling. The result at the top applies to year 3, when everything is running.
stages.year1:
Year 1

Cows, hens, fencing

  • 4 cows, 100 hens in one mobile henhouse, a few geese.
  • Electric fencing for the pasture, water along the laneway, a cattle shelter.
  • A dairy room in the old cowshed; register milk and egg sales with the county veterinary inspectorate.
  • A contract with an organic certification body before applying for payments.
  • Soil and hay testing; the first rotation.
  • Keep records: litres, eggs, hours, spending.
stages.year2:
Year 2

Sheep and cheese

  • Hens up to 200 (a second henhouse), if the eggs are selling.
  • 10–15 ewes, a night pen, a livestock guardian dog.
  • A cheese room and farm retail registration; cheese from summer milk.
  • A full three-field rotation, the farm’s own grain for the hens.
stages.year3:
Year 3

Meat poultry and decisions

  • A trial batch of 100 pastured broilers, once there is somewhere to slaughter them legally.
  • Goats for the scrub; pigs for the household, if the African swine fever situation allows.
  • A fifth cow or more sheep, depending on what sells better and how much hay is left.
  • Your own heifers from the best cows.

regulations.title: Law and formalities
regulations.intro: A summary of the most important matters. Regulations change, so before each start confirm the details with the county veterinary inspectorate (PIW) in Lwówek, with ARiMR and with the agricultural advisory centre (ODR).

notes.subsidies:
ARiMR and payments

  • A producer number and a herd registration; cattle, sheep, goats and pigs ear-tagged and registered; register the poultry flock too.
  • Leasing: payments, including the organic one, go to the tenant who actually farms the land. For the organic payment the lease should cover the whole commitment period. Put the lease in writing.
  • A payment application every year. The sheep payment is counted from 10 head, goats from 5 (check the thresholds).
  • Rates in the planner: direct and livestock payments are 2026 estimates (advance rates), animal welfare 2024, areas with natural constraints 2026, the organic payment 2023 estimates.
notes.organic:
Organic farming

  • A contract with a certification body and a conversion period (the payment is also available during conversion).
  • Hens: at most 6 hens per m² of henhouse, outdoor range, no synthetic amino acids, up to 5% non-organic feed.
  • Organic broilers: slaughter at the earliest on day 81, or slow-growing breeds.
notes.milkEggsCheese:
Milk, eggs, cheese

  • Raw milk and eggs: direct sales; notify the county veterinary officer at least 30 days before starting and get a veterinary number.
  • Eggs at a market: marking with the producer code is usually required (confirm with PIW).
  • Lamb: slaughter in an approved abattoir (a farm or service abattoir, in your own or a neighbouring county), meat with a health mark. The farm retail limit for red meat was 2,300 kg a year (2016 regulation). Whether you can sell whole carcasses or only after cutting in your own farm retail kitchen, confirm with PIW.
  • Cheese: farm retail (RHD), quantity limits are set by the veterinary officer’s decision. Farm retail revenue is tax-free up to 100,000 PLN, above that a 2% flat tax.
  • Do not advertise that milk “heals”: health claims on food are strictly regulated in the EU.
notes.poultryAndPigs:
Meat poultry and pigs

  • Poultry and rabbits slaughtered on the farm are sold under direct sales (notify the county veterinary officer). To make products from them you also need farm retail registration.
  • Sheep, goat and pig meat for farm retail products must come from an abattoir; meat from slaughter for own use is not allowed.
  • Keep turkeys apart from hens (histomoniasis).
  • Hatching for your own flock does not require registering a hatchery; selling chicks or hatching eggs does (county veterinary officer).
  • A winter tunnel during a poultry housing order: all openings covered with netting, feed and water inside.
  • Pigs: check the African swine fever zone with PIW. Biosecurity rules apply, and feeding kitchen scraps is prohibited.
  • Bird flu: during risk periods poultry must be housed, so mobile henhouses need a netted or closable option.
notes.produceBeesEducation:
Vegetables, bees, activities for children

  • Vegetables sold directly: ask the county sanitary-epidemiological station about registration.
  • An apiary must be registered with the county veterinary officer.
  • Cultivated mushrooms and juice from your own fruit: registration with the sanitary inspectorate (farm retail for plant food).
  • Activities for children (an educational farm): regular paid activities usually require a business registration (CEIDG), occasional ones may be unregistered; extra liability insurance is needed.
notes.processingAndShipping:
Products and shipping (farm retail)

  • Farm retail allows selling to consumers at a distance, including by mail order, as long as safe conditions, including temperature, are kept in transport. Selling through intermediaries is not allowed.
  • Farm retail quantity limits apply only to supplies to shops and restaurants (e.g. meat products 1,400 kg a year). Sales to consumers have no quantity limit.
  • Tax relief: at least 50% of the ingredients (excluding water) from your own farm; revenue up to 100,000 PLN is tax-free, above that a 2% flat tax.
  • In 2026 the ministry announced the removal of territorial restrictions and higher limits; the draft was under consultation. Check what has come into force before starting.
notes.wolvesBuildingsManure:
Wolves, buildings, manure

  • Wolf damage is compensated by the Regional Directorate for Environmental Protection; report it straight away, and shut sheep and goats in at night.
  • Shelters: ask the county office whether a notification is enough or a building permit is needed.
  • Manure and deep litter: storage according to the nitrates action programme (ask at the ODR).
notes.taxesAndInsurance:
Taxes and insurance

  • Selling unprocessed products (raw milk, eggs, live animals) is usually agricultural activity; products under farm retail as above. Confirm with an accountant.
  • KRUS, building insurance and the farmer’s liability insurance are in the planner’s fixed costs.

assumptions.title: Assumptions and sources
assumptions.method:
How it is calculated

  • A Jersey cow eats about 15 kg of dry matter a day (5.5 t a year), a heifer 3.3 t, a ewe with lambs 0.8 t, a goat 0.6 t.
  • Hen: feed ad lib, about 90% of it the farm’s own grain and pulses, the rest minerals and shell grit (bought).
  • Hay: 75% of the meadow yield goes to hay, 25% is regrowth for grazing; 70% of the pasture surplus can be cut.
  • Grain and hay from your own fields are valued at their growing cost, without rent for the land. Grain fed to hens could be sold for more, so what the eggs “earn” also includes that profit.
  • LU: approximate conversion factors (cow 1, heifer 0.6, sheep and goat 0.1, hen 0.014).
  • “Net” is the result before paying yourself for your work, without loan costs and taxes.
  • The “pessimistic scenario” is your current settings made worse by the sliders in that group: prices, yields, animal output, hours and costs. Rent stays the same.
  • Products are assigned to the species they come from (geese, ducks, sheep), together with a share of the smokehouse and shipping.
  • The work norms are my estimates for a small farm with a bucket milking machine. Correct them after the first year from your own records.

ryeWithVetch.name: Winter rye with hairy vetch
ryeWithVetch.timing: After harvest, by 1 October. Before oats with peas.
ryeWithVetch.purpose: The most reliable: it overwinters, the vetch fixes nitrogen, the rye protects the soil. Sheep grazing in autumn and from mid-February, then ploughed in before sowing oats.

landsberger.name: Landsberger mixture
landsberger.species: winter vetch, crimson clover, Italian ryegrass
landsberger.timing: Sown August – September. Before a late-sown crop or vegetables.
landsberger.purpose: In May it gives a cut of green forage or haylage for the cows, but that is too late for oats. Good before vegetables.

cloverUndersown.name: Clover undersown in oats
cloverUndersown.seeding: red clover 8–12 kg/ha, ryegrass or timothy 4–8 kg/ha
cloverUndersown.timing: April, together with the oats and peas or straight after.
cloverUndersown.purpose: Counts as an undersown crop (keep at least 8 weeks after harvest). It becomes the clover field in the rotation straight away.

winterTurnipRapeRye.name: Winter turnip rape with rye
winterTurnipRapeRye.timing: After harvest, by the end of August (turnip rape needs time before winter). Before oats.
winterTurnipRapeRye.purpose: Plenty of forage for autumn grazing by sheep and geese (October–November), overwinters. Turnip rape is a brassica: do not sow it if the rotation has brassica vegetables or oilseed rape.

multiSpeciesRye.name: Multi-species mixture with rye
multiSpeciesRye.species: oilseed radish, phacelia, vetch, crimson clover, oats or buckwheat
multiSpeciesRye.seeding: ready mixtures usually 25–40 kg/ha plus rye 30–50 kg/ha
multiSpeciesRye.timing: After harvest, August. Before oats or vegetables.
multiSpeciesRye.purpose: The most soil life: different roots, flowers for bees. Part of it is winter-killed, the rye stays green until 15 February. More expensive seed.

triticaleWinterPea.name: Triticale with winter field pea
triticaleWinterPea.timing: September. Before a late crop or vegetables.
triticaleWinterPea.purpose: In May green forage or haylage rich in protein. Like the Landsberger mixture: too late before oats.

phaceliaBuckwheatSerradella.name: Phacelia, buckwheat, serradella
phaceliaBuckwheatSerradella.timing: After an early harvest, July – August.
phaceliaBuckwheatSerradella.purpose: Fast, good for honey (bees), winter-killed and leaves a mulch. For the eco-scheme add an overwintering species (e.g. rye), because the cover must last until 15 February.

columns: Stubble cover crop (before a winter cereal, no payment)

whiteMustard.name: White mustard
whiteMustard.timing: Straight after harvest, July – early August; plough in in September before sowing the winter cereal.
whiteMustard.purpose: The cheapest and fastest, covers the soil quickly. A brassica: take care if you grow brassica vegetables.

phaceliaBuckwheat.name: Phacelia with buckwheat
phaceliaBuckwheat.purpose: Good for honey (bees), improves soil structure, not a brassica. Little forage.

oatsVetchPea.name: Oats with spring vetch and peas
oatsVetchPea.timing: After the earliest harvest (July), 7–8 weeks of growth.
oatsVetchPea.purpose: Green forage for the cows or sheep grazing in September, then ploughed in. The pulses fix nitrogen for the winter cereal.

nitrogen.title: Nitrogen and manure
nitrogen.intro: How much nitrogen the animals produce, how much they spread themselves on pasture and range, and how much stays in the manure to be hauled. Below, the balance of the fields and meadows the manure goes to. Approximate values, based on the nitrates action programme tables.
nitrogen.baleGrazingNote:
Bale grazing in winter

  • The bales are set out in autumn on a field that goes under a crop in spring, or on a poorer part of the meadow; somewhere different each year.
  • Not on waterlogged or flood-prone soil, nor by ditches and streams; during a thaw the animals move to a drier spot.
  • Access to water in winter (a heated trough or a water bowser) and shelter from the wind.
  • The nitrates action programme restricts fertilising in winter, so the site and the stocking rate are worth discussing with an ODR adviser.

risk.title: Risk in random years
risk.intro: How often the farm reaches its target when yields, prices, animal output and costs are a little different each year.
risk.chartLabel: Chart: how many years end with a given income
risk.method: The model recalculates the farm for 500 random years: each year has different yields, prices, animal output and costs, and roughly once in 20 years there is a bad year for the animals. Green bars are years with an income at least equal to the target, red ones below it. The pessimistic scenario is a single year in which everything goes wrong at once; it happens less often than the worst years on this chart. You set the variability in the “Pessimistic scenario” group.

customers.title: How many customers you need
customers.loyal: regular, taking a full basket (about {amount} PLN a month)
customers.occasional: if each bought only one product (about {amount} PLN a month)
customers.note: With regular families that is about {perWeek} hand-overs a week if each collects once a month, or one collection day for everyone. The first customers usually come through friends, the school, the parish and neighbours; the rest through recommendations.

nitrogen.total: Nitrogen from the animals in a year
nitrogen.onPasture: left by the animals themselves on pasture and range (about {perHa} kg/ha of pasture)
nitrogen.onBaleGrazing: stays in winter on the bale-grazing field
nitrogen.inManure: manure to haul: about {tonnes} t, about {hours} h of work
nitrogen.fieldsTitle: Fields and meadows with manure ({hectares} ha)
nitrogen.fieldsSummary: Manure gives about {manure} kg N, clover fixes about {clover} kg N, and grain, hay and root crops remove about {removed} kg N. Balance: {balance} kg N/ha a year.

fieldStatus.balanced: A balance close to zero: the fields do not get poorer and no nitrogen is wasted.
fieldStatus.surplus: A large surplus: some of the nitrogen will be leached. You can reduce the stocking rate, grow more cereals or give the manure to a neighbour.
fieldStatus.deficit: The fields are losing nitrogen: yields will fall over time. More clover in the rotation, catch crops with legumes or more manure will help.
